name: Bilal Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a roofing crew, four of us, for a firm that does roofs and loft conversions on older houses. Cut roofs, mostly, which means we build the roof from loose timber on the spot, not trusses from a factory. I'm usually up on the scaffold by half seven, marking out rafters with a pencil and a square my father gave me. Lunch is in the van, and home by five if the weather's kind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a hip roof. Getting all the angles to meet at the top, first time, no gaps, that still gives me a small kick after thirty-five years. What's hard is the cold, and the young ones who want to do everything with a phone app. My wife Samira keeps the books for a dental practice, and she says I'm the last man alive who still does sums on a timber offcut.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools, the chat programs and so on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I've never tried, and I don't really see why I would. My grandson showed me one that could write a poem about a cat, very clever, but it can't tell you if a purlin's going to sag. I'd rather keep doing things the way I know works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, a lot of noise about nothing. At work I'd probably not say much, maybe a joke at the van. I don't go online to talk about things like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I carry on as I am until I stop. I've got savings, and Samira and I own a small flat we rent out, so I'm not worried about money. I'd like to finish the way I started, with a pencil and a square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Do the jobs the firm gives us, keep my crew together. I'd plan to stop at sixty-two or sixty-three, whenever my shoulders say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as any other week, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the young ones on your crew say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf, he's twenty-four, would be a bit disappointed, he likes his gadgets. Adam would shrug. I'd tell them both that a good roof is a good roof, whatever's in your pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the job you'd be glad to see a machine do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carrying tiles up the ladder, maybe. That's a young man's job and it's never been mine for years. But they've had hoists for that since before you were born, so it's not new.

S0.say: A lot of noise about nothing. He'd make a joke in the van but wouldn't talk about it online.
S0.think: He carries on until he stops, secure with savings and a small rented flat he and his wife own. He'd like to finish the way he started, with a pencil and a square.
S0.do: Keeps doing the jobs the firm gives his crew and keeps the crew together. Plans to stop at sixty-two or sixty-three, whenever his shoulders decide.
S0.quote: I'd like to finish the way I started, with a pencil and a square.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal is short-spoken and settled, and this scenario simply confirms his plans. His identity is tied to old hand tools, including his father's square. He's dry rather than dismissive about the younger crew's gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not coming up a scaffold any time soon. People who sit at desks might need to worry, but a roof on a hundred-year-old house isn't the same twice. I'd say that at the van and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think it hardly touches me. Maybe the firm uses some program to price jobs, or to order timber. That's the office, it's fine. I've got a few years left, and old roofs don't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. Keep going, let the office get on with their computers. If the firm sent me on a course, I'd go, but I'd send Yusuf in my place if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little part of me wonders, but I don't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd send Yusuf in your place. Why not go yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he'll use it for forty years, and I'll use it for four. And because I'd sit there not understanding a word, and I'm too old to feel stupid in a room full of strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My eldest, Karim, is a driving instructor, so I'd ask if the self-driving cars are coming for him. He'd say not yet, Dad. My daughter's a pharmacist, and I'd tell her to watch it, that's the kind of work a computer could learn.

S1.say: It's not coming up a scaffold any time soon, because no old roof is the same twice. People at desks might need to worry.
S1.think: It hardly touches him: maybe the office uses software for pricing and ordering, and old roofs don't change in the few years he has left.
S1.do: Keeps working and leaves the computers to the office. Would go on a course if sent but would rather send his young crew member in his place.
S1.feel: Calm, with a small flicker of wondering.
S1.quote: I'd sit there not understanding a word, and I'm too old to feel stupid in a room full of strangers.
S1.fieldNote: Bilal's resistance has an honest root: he admits he'd feel stupid in a classroom. He sees his own work as safe and points worry at desk jobs, including his daughter's pharmacy work. He'd pass training to the younger worker, partly from fairness and partly to avoid it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it, not till I see a robot on a roof in the rain. At work I'd say let's see. If people were talking about it a lot, I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's true, it means I stop. I'd be sixty, and I'm not going to learn to run robots at sixty. We'd be all right, the savings and the rent from the flat, but I'd worry about Yusuf and Adam, they're young and roofing is all they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop spending on anything big, we'd put off the new kitchen Samira wants. I'd keep working as long as the firm wanted me, then stop when they said. Then I'd wait and see what happens with prices and the flat before I did anything with our money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not the money so much, it's not knowing what I'd do all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do all day, if you imagine it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd fix things for the neighbours, probably, gutters and fences. I'd go to the mosque more. Samira would want me out of the house by ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see with your money. What would you be waiting for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether people still want to rent a flat, whether rents hold. I don't know anything about markets and I don't want to make a stupid move in a hurry. My father always said when you don't know, don't move.

S2.say: He doesn't believe it until he sees a robot on a roof in the rain. At work he'd say let's see and keep his head down.
S2.think: If true, he stops at sixty, because he won't learn to run robots at that age. Money is covered by savings and rent from the flat, but his two young crew members only know roofing.
S2.do: Puts off big spending, including the new kitchen his wife wants, and works until the firm lets him go. Waits to see what happens with rents and prices before touching their money.
S2.feel: Anxious, less about money than about not knowing what he'd do all day.
S2.quote: My father always said when you don't know, don't move.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario threatens Bilal's sense of purpose more than his money. His instinct is to freeze: cut spending, avoid decisions, wait. He pictures retirement as fixing neighbours' gutters and more time at the mosque, but it plainly unsettles him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same idea, with five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the last one, I'd say let's see. Five years, a lot can happen, and a lot of predictions don't come true. I'd say to the crew, do your work, keep your heads down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be sixty-three and probably finished anyway. So it's not really about me. I'd think about the lads, and my grandson, he's twelve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as planned, put a bit more aside each month, maybe a few hundred. I'd tell Yusuf and Adam to take whatever courses the firm offers, because they've got time. And I'd talk to Karim about whether the flat's worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A little worry in the back of my head, but nothing that changes my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any training yourself with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know it's stubborn, but I'm a roofer, not a computer man. Five years is the end of my working life, I'm not starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn to do something with his hands as well as his head. Maybe that's out of date, I don't know. But it's what I know.

S3.say: Let's see, because a lot can happen in five years and many predictions fail. He'd tell the crew to do their work and keep their heads down.
S3.think: He'd be sixty-three and finished anyway, so it's not really about him. He thinks about his young crew members and his twelve-year-old grandson.
S3.do: Keeps working as planned and puts a few hundred more aside each month. Tells his young crew to take every course the firm offers and talks with his son about whether to keep the rental flat.
S3.feel: Uneasy, a worry in the back of his head that doesn't change his day.
S3.quote: I'm a roofer, not a computer man. Five years is the end of my working life, I'm not starting again.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Bilal steps back from the threat and looks at others, especially his grandson. He's open about being stubborn and doesn't apologise for it. His advice is honest about its limits: he admits it may be out of date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, nobody knows. I'd say, I'll be retired, it's somebody else's problem. That's what I'd say, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's nothing. I'd be sixty-eight, sitting in the garden. I'd think about the grandson, he'd be twenty-two, and whether there's work for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd finish at sixty-two or sixty-three, hand the crew to Yusuf if the firm lets me. Maybe I'd teach him the hip roofs properly before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's too far away to feel much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's somebody else's problem, half joking. What's the other half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other half is it's my grandson's problem, and that's not a joke. But I can't do much about 2036 from a scaffold in 2026. I can teach him to work hard, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the people in charge to do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make sure the young ones have something to do. Not just money, something to get up for. I've seen men with nothing to do, and it's not good for them.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and nobody knows. Half joking, he'd say he'll be retired so it's somebody else's problem.
S4.think: At sixty-eight he'd be sitting in the garden. He wonders whether there'll be work for his grandson, who'd be twenty-two.
S4.do: Keeps his plan to finish at sixty-two or sixty-three and asks the firm to hand the crew to his young crew member. Teaches him hip roofs properly before he goes.
S4.feel: Calm, because it's too far away to feel much.
S4.quote: I've seen men with nothing to do, and it's not good for them.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts it beyond Bilal's horizon, and his joke about it being somebody else's problem covers real concern for his grandson. He wants young people to have purpose, not just money. Handing on hip-roof skills is his one concrete act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the two years. Not for the money, for the lads and for what I'd do with myself. I don't know what would help, honestly. Maybe if the firm kept some of us on to check the robots' work, the old ones who know what a good roof looks like.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you covered it. Only that people like me, we don't post things or go on marches, so you don't hear from us. That doesn't mean we don't think about it.

headlineQuote: People like me, we don't post things or go on marches, so you don't hear from us.
portrait: Bilal Farah is a 58-year-old lead roofer who builds cut roofs on old houses with his father's old square and has never tried an AI tool. He and his wife own a rented flat and have good savings, so money isn't his worry in any scenario. What unsettles him is losing his purpose and the futures of his two young crew members and his grandson. His instinct under pressure is to freeze: cut spending, wait and see, and avoid moves he doesn't understand. He sees the slower AGI pictures as beyond his working life and keeps his retirement plans unchanged.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, for his young crew and for what he'd do with himself, not for the money.
whatWouldHelp: He wasn't sure, but suggested firms keep experienced roofers on to check the robots' work.
